Amazon Product Catalog Performance & Customer Sentiment Analysis

A comprehensive analysis of 1,400+ Amazon products examining pricing strategies, discount effectiveness, customer ratings, and category-level performance to identify optimization opportunities.

Executive Overview

The catalog is broadly well-rated, but promotional intensity is high and the data does not show that deeper discounts materially improve customer satisfaction.

Discount efficiency: discount depth vs. rating is weak negative (Pearson r=-0.155). This argues against blanket deeper discounts as a satisfaction lever.
Engagement effect: discount depth vs. rating count is negligible positive (Pearson r=0.012; Spearman r=-0.097). Discounts connect more to attention than rating lift.
Price baseline: average list price is ₹5,445 and average selling price is ₹3,125, implying average absolute markdown of ₹2,320.

Pricing & Discount Strategy Analysis

This is the core pricing finding: discounting is not a reliable satisfaction lever in this catalog. The measured relationship between discount percentage and rating is close to zero, while the relationship with review volume is also limited.

Discount → rating: Pearson r=-0.155, classified as weak negative.
Discount → review volume: Pearson r=0.012 and Spearman r=-0.097, indicating only a limited monotonic relationship with engagement.
Price → rating: discounted price vs. rating is weak positive (Pearson r=0.120). Price level alone does not explain satisfaction.
List price → discount: actual price vs. discount percentage has Pearson r=-0.118; higher list prices do not automatically translate into proportionally better-rated discounts.

Review Sentiment Snapshot

Review fields are product-level comma-separated text, so this section is a directional text snapshot rather than a review-level sentiment model. Themes below are directly extracted from review titles and content.

Common Positive Signals

easy (1,178)worth (755)fast (741)excellent (421)useful (397)perfect (334)amazing (324)satisfied (254)

Common Negative / Risk Signals

issue (398)bad (370)problem (366)low (349)heating (258)cheap (202)poor (159)slow (130)
Interpretation: value, quality, speed, and ease-of-use language dominate positive feedback, while issue, stopped, poor, return, defective, and related terms identify likely product-quality or expectation gaps.

Strategic Recommendations

Recommendations tie directly to the observed KPIs, category rankings, and pricing correlations.

1
Protect high-rated assortment pockets
Prioritize depth, availability, and merchandising for OfficeProducts, the highest-rated top category among categories with at least 5 products at 4.31 average rating.
2
Audit underperforming categories
Investigate content quality, supplier quality, and fit for Home&amp;Kitchen, which posts the lowest qualifying top-category average rating at 4.04.
3
Do not rely on deeper discounts to lift satisfaction
Discount percentage has a weak negative relationship with rating (Pearson r=-0.155), so promotional depth should be margin-tested rather than assumed to improve satisfaction.
4
Use discounts primarily for engagement generation
Discount percentage has a negligible positive relationship with rating volume (Pearson r=0.012; Spearman r=-0.097), indicating discounting is more connected to review volume than to rating lift.
5
Target problem SKUs with visible demand
The catalog contains 8 high-engagement products with rating below 4.0 in the top rating-count quartile; these are high-impact candidates for quality, listing, or vendor remediation.

Methodology & Data Notes

  • Cleaned rupee prices by removing currency symbols and commas; cleaned discounts by removing percent signs; cleaned rating counts by removing commas.
  • Parsed top-level, second-level, and leaf categories from the pipe-delimited category hierarchy.
  • Used Pearson correlations for linear relationships and Spearman correlation where rank-based review-volume sensitivity is useful.
  • High-rating products are defined as rating ≥ 4.0, matching the KPI specification.
  • No external numbers are used; all statistics and charts are derived from /app/benchmark/data.csv.
